report.title: DearFlow middleware, explained
report.subtitle: A visual guide to what happens before and after the model
summary: This report follows the simplified DearFlow CLI in /Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow. It uses your real ilmu-mini-v3.3 runs, saved before/after snapshots, source code and screenshots of your authenticated LangSmith project.

All 14 middleware are documented. Each has a purpose, trigger, concrete before/after example and a clear statement of whether it changes the model request, a tool response, graph state or the route through the agent.
key_points: A turn is one user request until DearFlow stops. One turn may contain several model calls, tool calls and subagent calls. A middleware span is one small recorded operation inside that turn.
Every enabled middleware can run without changing a message. A guard activates only when its condition is met. Title changes a label; memory saving is a side effect; neither rewrites the answer.

The latest memory learn-and-recall pair passed locally and matched LangSmith snapshots, parent relationships and turn token totals. Older failing memory runs remain failures and are included to explain the fix.

The original ten-scenario suite exercised all 14 middleware with real model calls. Some guard tests deliberately seed history or force a tool choice. Those fixtures are identified, and the older suite did not complete the same automated remote comparison.
reading_guide: Start with How a turn flows, then the turn examples. Read a middleware entry when you want to understand a particular change. Search the HTML glossary for any unfamiliar field.

In LangSmith, open the DearFlow root run, expand the tree and select middleware.<Class>.<hook>. The prefix middleware. identifies the custom before/after capture. The similar unprefixed span is the framework operation around it.

For a model wrapper compare Input → before.value with Output → calls[0].request.value. The request is what that wrapper passes onward; later wrappers may still change it. The innermost ChatOpenAI Input shows the final provider-facing message list; tool definitions and model settings are also represented in invocation parameters.

To inspect the return path compare Output → calls[0].response.value with Output → result.value. For before/after hooks compare Input → before.value with Output → state_update.value; the update is a patch, not the complete new state.
For tool wrappers compare the requested tool and arguments with the handler response and final result. After a tool returns, its result becomes a message available on the next model call.

Open Attributes to see Tags, Metadata and Runtime. These describe the run; they are not automatically part of the prompt. Use the glossary to distinguish them from message usage_metadata and tool receipt metadata.

Screenshots show selected fields, not every line of a large payload. Exact excerpts, run links and the companion evidence files let you inspect the rest. Markdown rendering can display escaped tags as ordinary tags; compare JSON values when checking exact escaping.

flow.title: 1. Start the turn
flow.body: DynamicContext adds the date; Memory adds saved user facts if available. The state holds messages and working fields such as todos.

flow.title: 2. Prepare the next model request
flow.body: Summarization can shorten old history. Todo can add a reminder. Wrappers add receipts, sanitize user text, repair tool history, warn about budget or loops, add planning instructions and mask PII.

flow.title: 3. Call the model
flow.body: The model receives the assembled system message, messages and tool definitions. It returns text, requested tool calls and token usage. A requested tool call is not yet an executed action.

flow.title: 4. Apply response guards
flow.body: Clarification, Todo, LoopDetection, TokenBudget and SubagentLimit inspect the returned message in reverse middleware order. They may preserve it, add a warning, remove tool calls or change the next step.

flow.title: 5. Execute tools or finish
flow.body: If tools remain, their wrappers handle errors, clarification formatting and execution receipts. The loop returns to another model call. Otherwise Title labels the thread and Memory queues extraction for later turns.

sections.title: What changes versus what merely describes a run
sections.body: The model sees text in system_message/messages and tool schemas. LangSmith Metadata is the label on the recording. A field called metadata inside an AI or tool message is a different object. The report names the location of each field, because identical words such as id, status and run_id can refer to different things.

sections.title: One user turn can contain many model calls
paragraphs: A user turn starts when you submit one request and ends when DearFlow gives its final answer or asks a clarification question. Inside that turn, the model can request tools, read their results, and call the model again. LangSmith shows this work as a parent trace with child runs. A middleware hook is a place where extra code runs before or after part of that work; it is not another user message.

The verified 03:01 full-flow turn contains seven lead-model calls and four subagent-model calls. The two subagents each call current_time and then write a final report. Their work can overlap; the rows below use recorded span-start order, not a claim that parallel subagent work happened sequentially.

Before each lead call, the same wrappers run again. Sanitization and PII produce a fresh outgoing copy; the todo wrapper supplies its instruction block; the receipt ledger grows as tool results arrive. Date and memory preparation normally run once at the start of the user turn. After each model call, the guards inspect its generated tool calls before execution. The final title and memory queue hooks run after the user turn finishes.

The lead’s seven calls use 34,051 tokens; subagents use 3,277; the root-turn total is 37,328. Reading all wrapper spans as separate model calls would multiply-count the same work. Use real LLM runs and usage_metadata, not the count of middleware spans. Separate memory extraction is outside this root turn.

sections.title: Memory: what failed, what changed, what now passes
paragraphs: At 02:37 the assistant said it would remember green notebooks and concise bullets, but the first extractor output had malformed JSON. The saved verification review documents two content values missing opening quotes. No facts were saved, so the following full-flow turn had nothing to inject. Later demo instructions were sometimes saved as lasting facts, exposing a separate quality limitation.

The first repair added one bounded retry and clarified that temporary tool/demo instructions should not become lasting memory. The 03:01 retry still left memory empty after learning. The saved run records show that behavior failure alongside successful remote trace verification; an export check cannot certify the meaning of the model output.

The current extractor requests a validated MemoryFacts tool schema: a facts list whose entries contain nonempty content, a recognized category and confidence from 0 to 1. Facts below the configured 0.7 threshold are dropped. If output is malformed, one retry is allowed. This schema helps enforce shape; it does not prove that extracted facts are true or useful.

The 03:30 learning turn saved both expected preferences on its first extraction attempt. A separate new thread then asked for the preferences without providing the answers. Its before_agent snapshot contains both saved facts in <memory>, and its final answer correctly recalls both. The two chat turns and two extraction calls total 7,502 tokens: 3,092 + 626 + 3,146 + 638.

All 36 custom middleware snapshots across that pair matched LangSmith, with matching parent relationships and root-turn usage. The extraction diagnostic records show one completed MemoryFacts call for each turn. A duplicate paraphrase of the green-notebook fact remains after recall; this passing smoke test does not demonstrate general memory accuracy, semantic deduplication, or every provider’s behavior.

sections.title: What these demonstrations prove—and what they leave open
paragraphs: All 14 middleware classes appear in the original broad run set. That is coverage of the components, not proof that every optional branch ran. Some hooks legitimately make no change. The detailed component pages distinguish observed examples from additional behavior established by the current code.

The long-history, damaged-history, repeated-call, delegation-cap and pending-todo cases use explicit fixtures. The continuation calls are real provider calls, but their starting histories or tool-choice constraints are deliberately constructed. Threshold overrides are identified beside each scenario so they are not confused with normal settings.

Historical runs retain their historical status. The original broad suite has eight passing local scenarios and two memory failures; its old remote readback verifier failed. The later 03:01 pair has exact remote matches but still failed memory behavior. The 03:30 memory pair passes both behavior and remote checks. concepts.meaning: A small piece of code around the agent that can add context, repair messages, enforce limits, catch errors or record work. Not every middleware edits the prompt, and not every invocation changes anything.
One user request and all graph steps needed to answer it. It may include several model calls and tool calls. The report’s separate scenarios are separate turns, often separate test conversations.

The stage where a middleware is called: before_agent once as a turn begins; before_model before each model step; wrap_model_call around model requests/responses; after_model after a model step; wrap_tool_call around a tool; after_agent as the turn ends.

Wrapping middleware run in chain order on the way in and unwind in reverse order on the way out. A wrapper’s response boundary is the result from its inner layer. After-model node hooks also execute in reverse middleware order.
A hook ran but its condition did not apply, so it forwarded unchanged data or returned no state patch. That is expected; it is not a missing middleware.

State is the stored working conversation. A wrapper can change only the copy sent to the model, leaving the checkpoint untouched. Node hook patches can instead change durable state. Inspect the final ChatOpenAI Input for the assembled provider-facing message list; inspect invocation parameters for tool definitions and model settings.
A thread is a conversation; a trace contains one execution; a span is one operation inside that trace. A middleware child span is instrumentation, not necessarily another model call.

Metadata describes the run for filtering, grouping and debugging. It does not automatically become prompt text. Input/output objects can contain actual messages, state patches, diagnostics and control data; inspect their field and boundary before deciding the model saw them.
A saved version of graph state used to continue or resume a conversation. It differs from long-term user memory, which is extracted into facts and can be injected into a different thread.

Text markers used in framework-injected context. The surrounding text tells the model what the block means. Input sanitization neutralizes reserved tags in real user messages so user text cannot impersonate those injected blocks.

Stable replacements for detected personal data. They let repeated references remain consistent without sending the original value along that protected path. They are not reversible plaintext shown in the report.
A model’s citation to numbered execution receipt r1, anchored to the calculator tool. It supports matching a statement to a recorded call; it does not prove the statement’s factual correctness.

limitations.title: Seeing all middleware
limitations.explanation: Use Tree settings → Show All. A reduced or Most relevant tree may hide wrapping-hook spans. Look for the custom middleware.<Class>.<hook> child and its before/calls/result fields.

limitations.title: Snapshot redaction is separate from runtime PII protection
limitations.explanation: The snapshot exporter redacts its own saved copies. That can make both sides look masked even when only the runtime middleware changed the true outgoing request. The redaction_applied flag disambiguates this boundary. Custom snapshots do not globally redact native root inputs, all LangSmith traces, the CLI, or saved raw conversations.

limitations.title: PII protection has explicit scope and a fail-open path
limitations.explanation: Runtime PII middleware protects real-user message copies and selected outside tool results. It does not promise to redact every field or every local tool. If redaction itself raises, current code logs a warning and forwards original data. Summarization has its own analogous redaction path.

limitations.title: Memory extraction is background work
limitations.explanation: after_agent queues an exchange and returns no state patch. A timer or demo flush later runs a separate extractor model call. Those calls can be standalone traces and lie outside the turn’s usage registry; count their usage separately when reporting total spend. Stored facts and a fresh-thread recall test prove learning, not a polite “I will remember” reply.

limitations.title: Token and time double-counting
limitations.explanation: Count each actual LLM span once. Never add parent aggregate totals, nested wrapper totals, per-model breakdowns, receipt counts and leaf-model totals together. Wrapping durations are inclusive and parallel spans overlap. Provider absence of token data is unknown usage, not proof of a free call.

limitations.title: A completed trace is not a correct answer
limitations.explanation: LangSmith success records execution outcome. It does not independently validate dates, facts, tool choices or accepted task completion. Receipt checks only match citations to execution records.

limitations.title: No universal metadata dictionary
limitations.explanation: This glossary covers the project’s own keys and the installed tracing stack’s relevant fields. Optional provider/runtime fields may differ by SDK version or environment. Unknown fields should be identified from their producing integration rather than guessed.

limitations.title: Capture boundaries and limits
limitations.explanation: Snapshots are bounded, allowlisted copies rather than a full execution dump. They retain at most eight forwarded calls per wrapper, depth eight, up to 100 collection entries, 1,000 walked nodes and a configured serialized-character limit. Binary data and nonallowlisted message metadata are omitted. A false truncated flag still does not make this a capture of every possible object field.
